query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-depositing a thin hafnium coating on a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of a dense, adherent HfO2 scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby reducing oxygen ingress and overall oxidation compared to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a VZrHfNbTa-type alloy) that normally forms porous or non-protective oxide scales when exposed to extreme temperatures in air.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin hafnium coating (via techniques such as hot-press sintering or vapor deposition) on the alloy surface before high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Exposure in an air atmosphere at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours under static conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The hafnium layer reacts rapidly with oxygen to form a continuous, dense HfO2 oxide layer; additionally, diffusion of zirconium into the coating forms an interfacial HfZr transition layer that strengthens the adhesion between the protective oxide and the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The pre-applied hafnium coating oxidizes preferentially to form HfO2, a thermodynamically stable and slow-growing oxide. This oxide acts as a physical barrier that limits further oxygen diffusion into the alloy, reducing internal oxidation and phase degradation at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation weight gain (on the order of approximately 40–50% reduction) and a smoother, less degraded surface morphology compared to an uncoated sample when both are exposed at 1600 °C in air for 5 hours.
generation.baseline: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, which develops a more porous and thicker oxide scale under identical high-temperature oxidation conditions, resulting in higher weight gain and surface degradation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under high-oxygen partial pressures and extreme temperatures (around 1600 °C); its benefits at lower temperatures, in cyclic thermal conditions, or in environments with different reactive atmospheres are not yet established.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., the percent reduction in weight gain and improvement in mechanical stability) and the long-term adherence of the HfO2 layer under variable thermal cycles remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical refractory HEA samples (e.g., VZrHfNbTa alloy): one group with a pre-deposited hafnium coating and an uncoated control group. Expose both groups to air at 1600 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform comprehensive microstructural and weight gain analyses.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis to quantify weight gain due to oxidation
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with EDS to assess oxide scale morphology and composition
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify protective oxide phases (especially HfO2)
Hardness measurements to evaluate any mechanical property improvements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hafnium-coated samples do not exhibit at least a 40% reduction in oxidation weight gain and do not show a denser, more adherent oxide scale (HfO2-based) compared to the uncoated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Preparation of VZrHfNbTa High-Entropy Alloy-Based High-Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Coating and Its Bonding Mechanism

Abstract: Ultra-high Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Alloys (UTORAs) have received a lot of attention due to the increased research demand for deep space exploration around the world. However, UTORAs have the disadvantages of easy oxidation and chalking. So, in this study, a UTORAs is prepared by hot-press sintering on VZrHfNbTa (HEA: High Entropy Alloys can generally be defined as more than five elements by the equal atomic ratio or close to the equal atomic ratio alloying, the mixing entropy is higher than the melting entropy of the alloy, generally forming a high entropy solid solution phase of a class of alloys.) a substrate coated with hafnium. The bonding mechanism, resistance to high-temperature oxidation, and hardness of the sample tests are carried out. The results show that zirconium in the matrix will diffuse into the hafnium coating during the high-temperature sintering process and form the HfZr alloy transition layer, the coating thickness of the composite is about 120 μm, and the diffusion distance of zirconium in the hafnium coating is about 60 μm

An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
